e.t: This word means “goodness,” referring to the quality of being good and upright. As a noun, it names goodness as a character or moral quality rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs four times, appearing three times in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the presence or expression of what is genuinely good.

Ain, also rendered En, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named biblical referent in the Greek Old Testament, while the available lexical definition does not provide a fuller sense beyond the name itself. This LXX word occurs five times, in Kings, Nehemiah, and Psalms. Its precise referent in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

ἀληθεύω means to be true or to tell the truth. It is a verb describing truthful speech or the expression of what is true, rather than deception or falsehood. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears five times, so it is relatively uncommon there. Its basic sense is straightforward: a person speaks truthfully or something proves true. The surrounding words determine whether the emphasis falls on telling the truth or being true in a particular passage.

This LXX noun refers to whiteness, specifically a white leprous skin condition. It names the visible whiteness associated with the condition rather than describing a person or an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Leviticus 13:39, within the law’s discussion of skin appearances. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the whiteness connected with white leprosy.

This noun means “reaping,” the gathering of a crop after it has grown. It refers to the harvest activity itself rather than to a person who performs it or to the field being harvested. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 23 times, showing that it is a recurring agricultural term. It appears in passages associated with Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Kings, Proverbs, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “engrave and set up.” It describes the act of putting words, names, or records into a lasting form and then establishing or displaying them. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs three times in the deuterocanonical Greek corpus, in 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being engraved and set up there.

“Unworthily” describes doing something in a manner that does not fit the value, dignity, or proper standard of the matter involved. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person or thing. This Greek LXX word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:42. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is acting in an unfitting or undeserving way.

This verb means “send back”: it describes directing a person or thing back to a previous place, person, or situation. It is a straightforward action word, and its precise force in a sentence depends on what is being sent and where it is sent. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Kings 21:10, so its normal meaning is clear even though its broader range of use is limited.

This noun means “firstfruit”: the first or earliest produce of a harvest, regarded as something set apart or presented. It names the initial yield rather than the whole harvest. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 72 times, especially in passages concerning Israel’s offerings and sacred portions. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains the firstfruit of what has been produced.

This Greek LXX verb means “turn off.” It describes the action of turning aside from a direction or route rather than continuing straight ahead. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, once in 2 Samuel and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a change of direction or course.

Asia is the name of a geographic region. As a proper noun, it identifies a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs nine times across eight verses, appearing in 1–4 Maccabees. Its repeated use points to Asia as a recognized regional designation in the historical setting of these books. The word itself names the region; the specific people, cities, or events associated with it must be understood from the surrounding passage.

“Unguardedly” describes doing something without protection, caution, or watchfulness. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out: openly or without taking precautions against danger. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezekiel 7:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is acting without being guarded or on alert.

Baitharam, also rendered Vetharam, is a proper name for a place rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 13:27. Because it functions as a place name, its meaning is primarily identifying a location named in the biblical account, not expressing a general concept or instruction. The precise significance of that location comes from the surrounding passage and its broader setting in Joshua.

Bala, also rendered Vala, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or place named in the biblical genealogical and territorial records. This name occurs four times across three verses, appearing in Genesis and Joshua. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it marks the particular name Bala wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse determines whether the name refers to a person or a location.

This word is the personal name “Beseleēl,” also rendered “Veselil.” As a proper name, it identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, with most occurrences in Exodus and additional occurrences in 1 and 2 Chronicles. The name appears especially in passages connected with the construction and furnishings of the tabernacle, though its precise significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “heavy,” describing something that has substantial weight or presses down. As a verb, it expresses the condition or effect of being heavy rather than naming an object itself. It occurs once in the Greek text of the Septuagint, in Wisdom 9:15. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains heaviness or weight.

Gaibel, also rendered Yevil, is a proper name used for a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but an individual name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance beyond identifying the person is not provided here, so the safest meaning is simply the personal name “Gaibēl” or “Yevil.”

This verb means “flatter”: to speak or act with pleasing praise toward someone, often in a way intended to win favor rather than simply state the truth. It describes an action, so it tells what someone does rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Proverbs 35:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX verb means “testify against”: to give testimony that stands as an accusation against someone. It describes a verbal act of bearing witness in opposition to another person, rather than simply offering neutral information. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Genesis 43:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains a testimony directed against someone.

This noun refers to an arrangement or pact—an agreed ordering or binding agreement between parties. Its central idea is something set in place or settled by agreement, rather than a casual choice or passing intention. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 13:25. The lexical sense is clear, while the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “teach”: to give instruction so that another person can understand or learn. It describes the act of communicating knowledge or guidance, whether a person teaches others or asks to be taught. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 94 times, showing a broad and recurring use for instruction. Its exact emphasis—such as what is taught and to whom—comes from the surrounding verse and passage.

δίφραξ refers to a seat or chair—something used for sitting. It is a noun naming a physical object, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 14:21. The available meaning is limited to this straightforward sense; the reference itself does not provide enough verse text here to explain any added contextual significance. Thus, when encountered, the word points simply to a seat or chair.

This Greek verb means “able” or “capable”: it describes having the power, capacity, or ability to do something. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:6. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its sentence, but its basic sense is the ability to accomplish or endure an action. It is a verb, so it expresses what someone can do rather than naming a person, object, or quality.

This verb means to look at or look upon someone or something. It describes directing the eyes toward what is being viewed, often with attentive observation rather than merely mentioning sight in general. In the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, it occurs three times: twice in Job and once in Isaiah. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation.

This verb means “wait” or “receive.” It describes either looking for someone or something to arrive, or accepting what is given. As a verb, its exact sense depends on what the sentence presents as the object: a person or thing may be awaited, or something may be received. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 15 times, showing use in both senses rather than a single fixed action. “Receive” is also represented in its English renderings.

This verb means to “uncover”: to remove what hides something so it can be seen or made known. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Proverbs.33.26. Its central idea remains straightforward: bringing something hidden into view. The surrounding verse would determine whether the uncovering is physical or figurative, but the word itself expresses the act of uncovering.

This Greek LXX noun means “rupture” or “bursting,” referring to a breaking open or sudden breaking apart. It describes an event or condition rather than an action someone performs. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezekiel 30:16. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains a breach, break, or bursting open. The word should therefore be understood as describing a forceful separation or breaking rather than a general weakness or ordinary opening.

This noun refers to a defect, a lack, or the loss of something. It describes what is missing, diminished, or suffered as a loss rather than naming an action. In its Greek LXX usage, it occurs seven times, all in Sirach, so its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording. The central idea remains a deficiency or loss: something falls short of what is complete, sound, or possessed.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Eliou” or “Eliu.” It functions as a personal name rather than a description, action, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s role or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the individual’s name, with the precise identity determined by the passage in which it appears.

Eliphas is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals named Eliphas in genealogical and narrative records. The name occurs 16 times across 15 verses, appearing in Genesis, Job, and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it tells the reader which person is being mentioned. The precise identity of each occurrence depends on its surrounding passage.

Emekachōr is a proper name, rendered as “Emekachōr” or “Emekakhor.” It is not presented here as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, but as the name of a specific entity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 7:24 and Joshua 7:26. The precise referent and significance belong to those passages’ surrounding text.

This adverb means “as far as possible,” describing an action carried out to the greatest extent circumstances allow. It qualifies a verb or statement by showing that someone does what can reasonably be done, without claiming that every desired result has been achieved. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 13:26. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense points to effort or action reaching the limits of what is possible.

This verb means to dream, describing the experience of dreaming during sleep. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for dreams experienced by people such as Jacob, Joseph, and Pharaoh, and it appears sixteen times across sixteen verses. The word can refer simply to the act of dreaming; the significance or message of a particular dream must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 28:12, and its latest is Joel 3:1.

This Greek LXX word describes something “of; lasting six months.” It points to a six-month duration or to something associated with that period. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 2 Kings and once in 1 Chronicles. Its basic sense is limited and precise: it marks a period of six months rather than expressing an action, quality, or spiritual theme. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what six-month period or connection is intended.

This Greek LXX verb means “incline”: to lean, turn, or direct something toward a person or thing. It describes an action or movement rather than a person or object. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and 1 Kings. Its broader force is to bend or orient oneself in a particular direction, while the exact sense in either passage depends on the surrounding verse. This word therefore expresses directed movement or a deliberate turning toward something.

This Greek LXX adjective means “seven thousand,” describing a quantity of 7,000. It functions as a number-word rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 3:39. The available lexical information establishes its numerical meaning, while the precise thing being counted must be understood from the surrounding verse. Thus, when encountered in a translation, it identifies the amount as seven thousand within that passage.

This noun means “finding” or “discovery”: the act or result of finding something. It can refer to something that has been located, recognized, or brought to light. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the uncovering or obtaining of something previously sought or not yet known.

This Greek LXX adverb means “peaceably,” describing the manner in which something is done. It points to conduct marked by peace rather than conflict or hostility. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 32:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a peaceful, non-contentious manner of acting. It functions by modifying an action or description, telling the reader that it happens peaceably.

This verb means “treat,” describing the act of providing something for another person, often in the sense of receiving or entertaining them. It presents an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:40. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what kind of treatment is meant there, but the word itself centers on treating someone. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L705737:identity; p03:word:lxx:L705737:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L705737:reference:0]

This word is a proper name, rendered “Ēra” or “Ira.” It identifies a person or named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, across 20 verses, including places in Psalms, Zechariah, and Ezekiel. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, the particular person or figure identified must be determined from each passage’s context.

This noun means “God,” referring to the divine being whom Scripture presents as Creator, Lord, and the object of worship. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used throughout the biblical story, from Genesis through the later writings, and appears 3,441 times in this Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus. Its normal function is to name or speak about God, while the surrounding passage determines the particular statement being made about him.

This verb means “harvest” or “reap”: to gather a crop from the field when it is ready. It describes the practical act of collecting what has grown, whether referring to grain or another agricultural harvest. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 25 times, chiefly in Old Testament books, and its central meaning remains consistent. The English rendering “reap” also reflects this basic sense.

Thorgama is a proper name used for a person or people-group named in the Greek Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, and no broader definition is provided here. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 10:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:6. These occurrences preserve the same name, “Thorgama.”

Iezlia is a proper name—a personal designation rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 8:18. The available information identifies the name as “Iezlia,” but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation for the name itself. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive horses” or “drive a chariot.” It describes the action of guiding or operating horses, especially when they are drawing or carrying a chariot. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Jeremiah 27:42. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the active driving of horses or a horse-drawn vehicle.

This word is a proper name identifying a Kaathite, also rendered Kaathitis. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:32. It functions as a name rather than a descriptive term, so its basic meaning is simply the designation of the Kaathite identified by it. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific role there.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the “character and conduct of a” person. It points to the way someone is characterized by what they do and how they behave. The wording of the definition is incomplete, so the surrounding verse is needed to identify the particular kind of character or conduct intended. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here: once in Psalms and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force therefore depends on the sentence in which it appears.

Kallai, also rendered Kalle, is a proper name rather than a word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:20. The name identifies a particular person in that passage, but the available verse text does not provide enough context here to say more about that person or the significance of the name. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the personal name “Kallai” or “Kalle.”

“Kappadokes” is a proper name for a people or group identified by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 2:23, and its lexical meaning is given as “Kappadokes” or “Kappathokes.” The word functions as a designation rather than as a description of an action or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This noun means a remnant: what is left over after part has been removed, lost, or separated. It can refer to people or a remaining portion, emphasizing what survives from a larger group or whole. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, most often rendered “remnant.” Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what or whom the surrounding context identifies as remaining.

This verb means to cover something with brass, describing the action of giving an object a brass covering. It names a practical physical action rather than a person, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 4:9. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what object is being covered there, but the word itself clearly expresses the act of covering with brass.

This verb means to “spy out” or “reconnoitre”—to examine a place or situation carefully, often to gather information before action. It describes purposeful investigation rather than casual observation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the deliberate scouting or inspection of something to learn what it is like and how it may be approached.

This Greek LXX noun means a “stain” or “spot”—a visible mark or blemish. It names something that mars or marks a surface, object, or person, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs two times in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Wisdom 13:14 and once in 2 Maccabees 6:25. Its central sense is a mark that soils or disfigures.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “hut” or a “group.” It can name a simple shelter or a collection of people considered together. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:31. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains centered on either a hut or an assembled group.

Maizoob, also rendered Mezoov, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 36:39. Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes a particular person or named figure from others. The form itself does not provide a broader concept or teaching apart from the person it names.

This word means a small sack or purse, a noun for a container used to carry things. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. The English rendering “purse” appears in two of its recorded uses, supporting the sense of a small money bag or carrying pouch. Its precise use in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective describes something connected with singing or music—something “singing; musical.” It identifies a musical quality rather than naming a person, place, or action by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 4 Maccabees 10:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is related to song, melody, or musical expression.

This adjective describes someone who reckons with trifles—treating small or minor matters as things to be counted, considered, or weighed. It presents a person’s habit or character rather than naming an object. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 14:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is attention given to matters that are trifling or insignificant.

“Moabite” identifies a person from Moab or describes something associated with Moab. As both a noun and an adjective, the word can name someone as a Moabite or modify a person or thing connected with Moab. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times across 17 verses, including several uses in Ruth and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to a wooded vale or dell—a low, sheltered place surrounded by or covered with trees. It describes a physical feature of the land rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times in eight verses, including passages from Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description, but its central meaning remains a wooded hollow or small valley.

This noun means “young of the deer; fawn,” referring to a young deer. It is an animal term used as a noun, not a title, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Song of Songs, where it consistently refers to a young deer. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear and concrete.

This noun means an admonition or warning: a spoken caution intended to correct, guide, or alert someone. It names the message itself rather than the act of giving it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 5:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a serious word of counsel or caution. The term therefore points to instruction that calls attention to a needed correction or to danger that should not be ignored.

This Greek LXX noun means “groom,” the man entering marriage. It refers to a bridegroom in the setting of a wedding and helps describe marriage-related relationships or imagery. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical books represented here, from Judges through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the man who is marrying or is married to a bride.

This verb means “make yellow,” describing the change of something into a yellow color. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Leviticus 13:30–32. Its use is connected with observing a visible change in a person's hair or affected area, though the precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording. The word describes a color change rather than naming a person, object, or condition by itself.

Ozan is a proper name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader action, quality, or idea; its function is simply as a personal name. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 6:26 and 1 Chronicles 7:24. The available lexical information gives “Ozan” as its meaning and does not provide an additional sense. Its precise reference in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text and context.

This word means “ear,” the bodily organ associated with hearing. It is a noun and can refer to one ear or to ears in the plural, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings of this corpus, it occurs 385 times, showing that it is a common word for this physical part of the body. Its normal meaning remains straightforward: the ear, or ears, through which hearing takes place.

“Palaestra” refers to a wrestling school or training place, especially a setting associated with wrestling. It is a noun naming a physical place rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:14. The word’s basic meaning identifies the place itself; the surrounding verse is needed to explain how that place functions in its particular context. This gives the reader a clear sense of the word without assigning it a broader spiritual or figurative meaning.

This Greek LXX verb means “take away from beside” or “withdraw.” It describes removing something or someone from a nearby position, rather than leaving it in place. As a verb, it expresses an action of taking away or drawing back. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains removal or withdrawal.

This word means “on the spot,” describing something that happens immediately or right at the moment in question. It functions mainly as an adverb, telling when an action or event occurs rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 17 times, showing a recurring way to express sudden or immediate timing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “leap” or “spring.” It describes a person, animal, or thing moving upward or forward with a sudden, lively motion. As a verb, it expresses the action itself rather than naming the person or object that moves. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, appearing once in Leviticus and once in Song of Songs. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an energetic leap or spring.

“Citizen” is a noun for a person who belongs to a city or civic community. It identifies someone as a member of a people or place, rather than merely describing a person’s location. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 17 times, including uses in Genesis, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “from afar,” describing something seen, heard, or happening at a distance rather than nearby. It can indicate physical remoteness and helps locate a person, object, or event in relation to the speaker or observer. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, with eight occurrences in Isaiah and others in Job, Jeremiah, 2 Kings, and Wisdom. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “space immediately in front of,” referring to an area situated before something else. It is a location term rather than the name of a person, object, or action. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Numbers 35, where it relates to the surrounding space associated with the Levitical cities. Its exact nuance in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is a space lying directly before or outside a place.

This Greek LXX verb means “predict” or “state before.” It describes saying something in advance, whether presenting what is expected to happen or declaring something beforehand. The word appears 11 times in the Greek LXX material represented here, across 10 verses, especially in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on what is being stated and the surrounding passage.

This verb means to afflict beforehand—to cause suffering or hardship before another point or event. Its wording focuses on the prior timing of the affliction, not merely on suffering in general. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:22. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, which are not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “stumble.” It describes a person or group encountering difficulty and losing steady progress, whether physically or in a broader sense. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including occurrences in Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and later deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains stumbling or failing to move forward steadily.

Ragma, also rendered Rhagma, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Amos 6:11. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding text to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise significance in Amos therefore depends on the verse and its broader passage, while its basic lexical function is simply to identify a named entity.

This noun refers to a dealer in petty wares—a huckster, someone who makes a business of selling small or low-value goods. It names a kind of tradesman rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah 3:31–32. The word’s basic meaning identifies the person’s trade; the surrounding verse is needed to determine what is being said about that person in either occurrence.

This noun refers to the Sabbath, and it can also mean a week. As the Sabbath, it identifies the appointed day of rest; as a week, it names a period of time. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 126 times, showing regular use for both the sacred day and the broader time expression. Its precise sense in a particular passage depends on how the surrounding sentence uses it.

Salamin is a proper name, identifying a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. Its meaning is simply “Salamin”; the word does not carry an ordinary descriptive sense like a common noun or verb. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 19:48 and Joshua 22:29. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

Samouias, also rendered Samoias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Chronicles 17:8. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is mainly its identification of a particular person in that passage; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role or significance. The name itself does not provide a broader teaching or concept apart from the person it identifies.

The word refers to a military standard or an organized body of troops. It is a noun describing the visible banner or grouped unit by which people are arranged for military movement or camp organization. Its stated meaning is “military standard; body of troops.” In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Numbers 2:2. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this summary gives the word’s ordinary meaning rather than explaining its specific force in that verse.
